en: New Commentary on the Treatises of Sengzhao,
Volume One Founder and Abbot of Dawań Shèngyòuguó Temple, Śramaṇa Yuán Dà;
Patriarch of Bǎimǎ Temple, Posthumously Honored as Duke of Guī State.

Written by the monk Wencái, a Master of the Sea-Seal Opening of the Dharma and a long-term lecturer: From the beginning, I have been fond of reciting this treatise and have roughly perused its phrasing;
yet, I have not yet been able to savor its profound principles and flavor with my own mind.
Furthermore, while serving at the Xingjiao Monastery in Liefan River,
he obtained the preface by Chan Master Yun’an Da; several years later, responding to a summons from Ningxia,
he again encountered Chan Master Tang Guangyao.
Furthermore, there are the commentaries of two masters, including Dharma Master Jingyuan of the Song dynasty;
however, through repeated comparison and collation,
their strengths and weaknesses appear so muddled and contradictory that it seems they have not fully captured the subtle excellence of the treatise’s intent.
Furthermore, its profound essence and concise depth have long been renowned;
its phrasing is elegant and its application is eloquent.
Unless one has deeply penetrated the true nature of reality and ascended to the pinnacle of skillful eloquence,
let no one attempt this.
I firmly consider it to be the great key that opens the Mahāvaipulya sūtras.
It is a great vessel for traversing the vast ocean of the nature of reality;
it is a balanced carriage for operating the power of expedient means;
and it is the correct teaching that dispels divergent views.
This is an elegant composition of the true Lion’s Roar of the One Vehicle.
Those who wish to study the nature of human beings should first apply themselves with diligence to this work.
If one penetrates it in this way, then the principle of the Great Dharma will be wondrously attained without being sought. Alas!
From the Yao Qin dynasty until the Tang, more than two hundred years passed.
Throughout the succession of sagely monks at Xianshou, Qingliang, and Guishan,
all have cited these [teachings] to resolve matters of great significance;
yet alone has no one elucidated their subtle essentials to summon those who would come after.
Consequently, various explanations have become as tangled as the handles of adzes,
such that no one knows the correct standard by which to adjudicate them.
Therefore, on a day of leisure, I have respectfully gathered the teachings of the former awakened ones.
I have separately prepared these exegeses to transmit to those under my guidance; I feel ashamed that, constrained by the exigencies of worldly affairs,
I am unable to devote the leisure and meticulous attention required for every time I cite sources to explain a meaning.
I hope that those who share my same robes and virtue will, out of compassion for my crude and inelegant errors, correct them.
*Zhao lun*: "Zhao" is the name of the author.
A "treatise" (*śāstra*) refers to that which has been composed;
it is a collective title for a body of work that unifies both the person [who authored it] and the doctrine [it contains].
Because these four treatises were produced at different times and each maintains its own distinct doctrine,
one wishes to synthesize them into a single whole.
It is impossible to survey them all;
therefore, he further composed a single chapter on the fundamental thesis and placed it at the beginning of the treatise.
It is simply that the commentaries on Sengzhao’s treatises all belong to this category;
as for what is called "discourse," it refers to the provisional establishment of interlocutors to resolve and determine matters of profound depth.
Through successive inquiry and investigation,
it demonstrates the cultivation and realization of phenomena;
therefore, it is called a *śāstra* (treatise).
However, there are two types:
the first is the treatise on tenets (*siddhānta-śāstra*), which establishes its doctrines based upon the scriptures.
Such as the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and so forth.
Second are the commentaries (*śāstra*),
which merely explain in accordance with the sūtras.
As in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other works,
these four treatises are the former rather than the latter.
This is stated in the *Tongjian* (Comprehensive Mirror), composed by Shi Sengzhao of Chang’an during the Later Qin dynasty.
Fu Jian occupied the Guanzhong region and styled his state the Great Qin.
Toward the end of Fu Jian’s reign,
Yao Chang usurped the throne and likewise styled his state Qin.
Therefore, the historians distinguished them by using the characters for "former" and "latter.
The Master of the Treatise lived during the Later Qin dynasty.
Chang'an is the present-day Anxi.
"Śākya" refers to Śākyamuni;
it is the common clan name of the Saṃgha,
as the Tathāgata belongs to the Śākya lineage.
Master Dao’an established the model;
it resonates with the Āgamas from afar.
For a thousand ages, it has been followed and relied upon.
To this day it has not ceased.
"Sengzhao" is the posthumous name of the author of the treatise.
His original biography states briefly:
A native of Jingzhao,
he had extensively surveyed the classics and histories and mastered the entirety of the ancient records;
his aspirations were directed toward the profound and subtle mysteries.
He constantly took Zhuangzi and Laozi as the essentials of his mind;
thus he sighed, saying:
"It is indeed beautiful, but it is merely so."
However, his method for dwelling the spirit beyond the fetters of the mundane was not yet fully perfected.
Later, upon seeing the old *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, he received it with joy and veneration, whereupon he said:
"Only now do I know where I truly belong."
Therefore, he left the household life to study the excellent Vaipulya sutras and became proficient in the Tripiṭaka.
Hearing that Kumārajīva was in Guzang, he [set out for him].
He followed him from afar;
Kumārajīva praised and admired him boundlessly.
When Kumārajīva arrived in Chang’an, [he likewise honored him].
Sengzhao also followed him into [the palace].
Yao Xing issued an edict ordering him to enter the Xiaoyao Garden to collate and finalize the sutras and śāstras.
He composed the *Four Treatises* as well as commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*.
He also composed prefaces for various sutras and treatises,
all of which have been transmitted to the world.
"Zuo" (作) means to produce or to create.
The *Yicheng foshuo lun* (Treatise on the Meaning Truly Spoken by the Buddha) was composed by [the author] himself;
it merely employs the phrasing while not fully embodying the underlying meaning.
Regarding the "Fundamental Doctrine" (*zongbenyi*): that which is venerated in the Four Treatises is called the "Doctrine" (*zong*).
"Fundamental" refers to both the universal [application] of phenomena (*dharma*) and their meaning (*artha*).
Regarding phenomena, there are both universal and specific types. As for the universal:
This is precisely the single mind of the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Master Jingyuan of Zhongwu stated:
"Now, these four treatises take this single mind as their fundamental tenet."
Nevertheless, although the four treatises differ,
each of them also expounds the meaning of this single mind.
As for their distinctions:
Thus, the tenets of the four treatises each differ.
The reason for this is that a single mind is required to encompass these four dharmas.
Without these four dharmas, there is no way to demonstrate the single mind.
Thus, the one is the four, and the four are the one.
"Meaning" (yi) refers to the principle (yili) that is manifested through the preceding dharma-substance as its phenomenal characteristics.
There is the universal Dharma and universal meaning, as well as the particular Dharma and particular meaning;
the significance of these four sections, according to their respective divisions,
constitutes the fundamental tenets of the four treatises that follow.
Accordingly, without the fundamental tenet there would be nothing to unify the four treatises;
without the four treatises there would be nothing to elucidate the fundamental tenet.
Thus, the Dharma is taken as the basis of what is held as the tenet.
The fundamental is based on meaning, and the fundamental is itself meaning.
If dharma and meaning are divided, when the fundamental belongs to dharma, it is the meaning of that fundamental. The fundamental lacks substantial characteristics;
it is the dharma-nature, which is empty by nature, arising through the convergence of conditions. These five names are found throughout all the sutras.
Although these meanings differ, they do not transcend the principles of phenomena (li) and events (shi).
Now, following their sequence from beginning to end, I shall briefly explain them.
"Initial" refers to the event of the convergence of conditions; prior to this convergence, there was nothing.
Therefore, it is said that they are fundamentally non-existent. The characteristic of non-characteristic is further called the "true characteristic" (bhūtalakṣaṇa);
this very true characteristic is the nature of all phenomena (dharmatā).
Therefore, it is called "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
Because this nature is true emptiness, it is further called "nature-emptiness" (prakṛti-śūnyatā).
Furthermore, because the principle of nature-emptiness is not separate from phenomena.
To engage with phenomena through principle is also termed the "convergence of conditions," meaning that all phenomena exist through the gathering of causes and conditions;
they may also be called the "assemblage of conditions" or "dependent origination," and so forth.
In all cases, the intent lies in the Dharma.
Master Dushun said: "Apart from ultimate truth, not a single thing can be found.
This is but a single principle; the principle is manifested by relying on the Dharma.
Since phenomena (dharma) are of a single source in both principle and fact,
how could their meaning allow for divergence? One must not grasp at the five names and calculate that there are five distinct dharmas,
each constituting a separate meaning.
In this context, to proceed from the root to the branches means that there are only branches and no root;
likewise, to subsume the branches back into the root means that there is only the root and no branches. These are two aspects of the same principle.
This is also a single meaning.
If the beginning and the end are interpenetrated such that their boundaries cannot be distinguished,
this is especially a single meaning.
If one explains this by not shifting the perspective downward:
conditions are the phenomena,
while the principle of fundamental non-existence is the equal reality.
Because of this single principle,
there is both transition and non-transition;
therefore, it constitutes the thesis of the "Treatise on Non-Transition" (Bùqiānlùn).
Why is this so? It is because it is a sign:
all phenomena arise through the convergence of conditions; whether form or mind, they arise only after causes and conditions have assembled.
Arising through the convergence of conditions, that which has not yet arisen does not exist;
when conditions disperse, it ceases. The first sentence follows upon the preceding [point]: causes are the conditions and all phenomena are the effects.
It is impossible for an effect to exist while its cause is absent.
This refers to the prior limit.

As for the subsequent phrase: since phenomena themselves arise through dependent origination and conditioned things undergo transition and cessation, when causes and conditions disperse, all phenomena perish and pass away.
This refers to the future limit.
If it were truly existent, then there would be no cessation; "truly" means "real.
If a phenomenon were substantially real, its existence should be without cessation.
Since the phenomenon perishes along with it,
one knows it is not truly existent.
As the subsequent treatise states:
If something were truly existent, how could it depend upon conditions to exist?
As the *Madhyamaka* states:
"If phenomena were substantially existent, they would not be subject to non-existence," and so forth.
Inferring from this,
one knows that although things presently exist,
their nature is eternally empty.
Because its nature is eternally empty of itself, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*); this reveals the fundamental through the derivative.
Contemplating present phenomena in relation to the prior and posterior limits, one sees that they arise solely as conditions from a collection.
How could it wait until conditions have separated before it then ceases?
Since causes and conditions are not in union and are thus eternally separate even now,
they cease even now.
Form is itself emptiness; its nature is thus from the beginning.
Therefore, that which arises through conditions is precisely the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
As the Holy Master Qingliang said:
That which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature; its very substance is itself the truth, because its nature is empty.
Therefore it is called "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*); true emptiness is the nature of all phenomena.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus;
therefore, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). "Thus" means emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Because emptiness is without marks (*animitta*), [it is the true mark].
Therefore, it is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The true mark is itself non-existent;
it is not made non-existent through deliberation.
Therefore, it is called "original non-existence" (benwu): the dharmas that arise through the gathering of conditions are fundamentally empty in their very substance.
Just as reflections in a mirror or echoes in a valley do not require further refutation to be made non-existent, this very suchness (shixiang) is original non-existence.
The lower treatise states:
"How could one wait for dissection in order to seek comprehension?
This distinguishes [the Mahāyāna] from the Hīnayāna practice of analyzing form (rūpa) to designate it as emptiness (śūnyatā).
The names listed above proceed from the root to the branches,
whereas the investigation of their meanings herein proceeds from the branches back to the root;
nevertheless, the root and the branches are fused into a single unity.
It is neither before nor after, neither one nor different.
Regarding the statement that it is "neither existent nor non-existent," many sūtras and śāstras extensively clarify the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
namely, existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence.
Neither existent nor non-existent;
according to the Dharma, the manifestation of virtue does not transcend these four.
Furthermore, regarding the refutation of conceptual constructions and the elimination of denials, there are also four propositions:
namely, neither existent nor non-existent, nor non-non-existent;
neither non-non-existent nor both existent and non-existent.
Regarding what is now cited—
the fourth [verse] from the preceding section and the first two lines of the following section—
the reason for specifically citing these to provide clarification is as follows:
To dispel the two views,
to reveal the Middle Way by way of negation,
and to cause the mind to abide nowhere— these constitute the core tenets of the *Treatise on Non-Being in the Ultimate Sense*.

"It is not that there is truly existence for those with the view of eternalism, nor non-existence for those with the false views of annihilationism. This first section explains by way of refuting such conceptualizations.
The *Buddhatva-śāstra* (Treatise on Buddha-nature), fascicle three, states:
All views do not transcend the two types of existence and non-existence.
Because of the view of existence, one clings to permanence;
within the view of non-existence, there are furthermore two types.
First is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*),
which refers to the total denial of cause and effect as well as the three periods of time.
Second is the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), which refers to believing only in the present and disbelieving in the future.
By analogy with this, there are two [extremes]: eternalism based on the cause of birth, and nihilism based on the cause of non-birth;
therefore, the treatise presents both together.
In the Sūtra, in order to refute this view, it is stated that things are neither existent nor non-existent.
The Commentary explains:
"This differs from the view that calculates existence; it is not the 'existence' of the eternalist view."
Therefore it is said:
"The 'non-existence' that differs from various conceptualizations is not the non-existence of wrong views or the view of annihilation."
Therefore, it is said that they are "not non-existent.
This is not like the two preceding statements which govern the subsequent "false severance" (邪斷).

If one holds that "existence" implies permanence, then one must hold that "non-existence" implies annihilation. Since existence is not truly existent, non-existence is likewise not non-existent. This is an explanation based on arising and ceasing.
The first two phrases clarify that [these views] arise through mutual causality;
they simply give rise to one view, and from that one view, others follow in succession.
This is like seeing that a cow has horns and consequently asserting that a rabbit has no horns, and so forth.
Thus, the *Ghanavyūha* states:
"To depend upon the existence of phenomena and thereby give rise to the view of non-existence—
this is the affliction that must be remedied."
The latter two phrases clarify that they perish through mutual causation;
if one view is rectified, that view will accordingly vanish.
Since the sutra already states that they are "not existent," [how could they be established?]
Therefore, it is also not non-existent.
Thus, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says:
"Since dharmas are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning, what could the view of non-existence depend upon?"
This is the medicine that can counteract [the afflictions].
How magnificent! Your skillful means exhaustively realize the intent of the sutras.
As for those who wish to preserve [the Dharma] yet still grasp at it, they have no way to contemplate the dharmas.
This may be called knowing the true reality (*dharmatā*) of phenomena.
It means that although one contemplates existence, there is no grasping at signs. This is an explanation in terms of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).

The Dharma refers to all phenomena arising through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*). This means that although these phenomena are empty by virtue of their dependence on conditions, one cannot maintain a state of mere non-existence when contemplating them.
If they were simply non-existent, then the Three Trainings, the Six Perfections, and even the five heinous crimes and ten unwholesome actions would be empty and bear no fruit.
Because they are not non-existent, all phenomena are established.
Regarding "not grasping at signs":
although dependent origination exists, one should not grasp at its signs when contemplating it.
If one grasps at things, they arise and perish through conditioned activity; how can such practice accord with the Truth?
Because [all things] are not-existent, the mind does not dwell upon appearances.
To establish a single merit or cultivate a single virtue, there is nothing that does not harmonize with the Way.
Only by seeing the Dharma in this way does one recognize the true mark (*tathatā*).
The term "true mark" refers to what follows in its meaning;
it is precisely the contemplation of the Middle Way and Buddha-nature.
The underlying intentions herein are boundless and cannot be recounted in detail,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and other texts.
The three preceding points explain the etymology of the name.
The first two [stages] involve leaving behind, while the latter one constitutes the accomplishment of practice.
Thus, the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are the characteristics of signlessness;
the mind of the sage dwells in non-dwelling. As for these "characteristics of phenomena": [The text continues: "Characteristics of phenomena" refers to...
The object of contemplation belongs to the aforementioned true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Since it is neither existent nor non-existent, how could it possess any phenomenal characteristics?
Furthermore, it is in contrast to the mind that does not abide.
Because their meanings and characteristics are thus,
it is called "the characteristic of no-characteristic.
Regarding "the sages and so forth":
The mind capable of such contemplation attains non-discrimination;
both are termed "sages.
However, those prior to the [first] stage who cultivate the samādhi of True Suchness (tathatā) [are as follows].
It is also permitted to emulate the practice of simultaneously illuminating both existence and non-existence, which is called "abiding.
Since one neither retains non-existence nor grasps at signs, this is abiding while being without abiding.
Although those who practice the School of Nature (Xingzong) may be ordinary persons bound by all fetters,
if they have been cultivated by past impressions, they should certainly devote their attention to it.
I now cite the Sage’s mind so that people may admire and follow its example.
The three vehicles equally contemplate the emptiness of nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā) and thereby attain the Way.
"Emptiness of nature" refers to the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena. "Equally" means with equality.
The "Path" refers to the enlightenment of one's own vehicle.
The reason for distinguishing it in terms of persons is to prevent the doubt that,
apart from the true reality (dharmatā), there might be separate and distinct realizations for the three vehicles.

Yet they do not realize that while the capacities of the three vehicles differ according to their respective karmic perfuming, the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) that is observed is without distinction.
Therefore, Śāriputra said:
"We have entered equally into the dharma-nature."
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa for their identical liberation,
just as three animals crossing a river encounter no difference in the water.
Because they perceive the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is called "right contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*).
If they were different, it would constitute a false contemplation; the two contemplations—correct and false—are explained throughout the various sutras.
Now, we distinguish between the false and the correct based on the true nature (*dharmatā*).
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Apart from the true nature of reality (dharmatā), everything else is the work of Māra.
Even if those of the two vehicles do not perceive this principle, they are nonetheless inverted. Regarding this, there are two explanations.
The first refers simply to the two vehicles within the three vehicles.
The meaning is:
even if one follows the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and does not perceive the principle of the emptiness of nature.
Thus, they are also inverted and unable to realize the fruit of fruition.
This is because the followers of the Two Vehicles see only impermanence and do not see permanence; this constitutes their inversion.
This can be explained by means of the correspondence between large and small forms;
it is already so in the case of the Small Vehicle, let alone the Mahāyāna.
Secondly, the previous mention of the "Three Vehicles" refers to those taught by the Shared Teaching who study the emptiness of dharmas; therefore,
they equally take the contemplation of the true reality (dharmatā) as their correct contemplation.
These two vehicles are now those of the "Dull-Witted" (yūhō) who are the objects of the Tripitaka Teaching (zangkyō).
The meaning is this:
even if they are of the dull-witted two vehicles, they must also contemplate the principle of the emptiness of nature (shōkū no ri) in order to attain realization.
If one does not perceive this principle, one will be inverted and thus fail to realize it.
The Great Commentary (Dàshù), in refuting the teachings that maintain [the existence of] phenomena, cites the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, saying:
"I shall now correctly elucidate the true meaning within the Tripiṭaka."
Ultimate reality is emptiness.
The *Qingliang chao* states:
"One cannot attain the Way without perceiving ultimate reality."
Since the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is also one part of the twofold emptiness,
how could there be such a great difference?
Therefore, it was previously stated that they are "equally contemplated."
Therefore, the observation of phenomena by the three vehicles is no different;

there is only a distinction based on whether the mind is great or small. The ultimate reality toward which they proceed is one and the same, yet differences arise from the capacities and dispositions of those who proceed.
Vessels have varying capacities, and wisdom has varying depths;
there are differences between self and others in practice, and between circuitous and direct paths in progress;
likewise, there are single and double realizations. These discrepancies lie in the person, not in the Dharma.
"Upāya-prajñā" is a designation for "Great Wisdom.
Both terms are cited together to collectively refer to its essence.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 18, states:
Mahāprajñā is translated in the Qin language as "Great Wisdom" (Dahui).
Upāya is here translated as "Skillful Means."
Because it unifies both in a single thought-moment, it is called "Great Wisdom" (Mahāprajñā).
The wisdom of the two vehicles is solitary and individually sharp, yet it is not "great.
This constitutes the central tenet of the entire treatise, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
To perceive the true reality of phenomena is called *prajñā*.
That it can manifest without taking form is the merit realized through *upāya*. The first two phrases clarify the origin of its name:
it is called *prajñā* because it perceives the true reality.
The latter two lines indicate seeing but not realization;
it is solely through the guidance of great compassion that wisdom is led so as not to realize emptiness.
This refers to transcending the two vehicles.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Wisdom devoid of skillful means is bondage; wisdom endowed with skillful means is liberation."
Because they are intoxicated by the wine of nirvana with wisdom devoid of compassion,
they fall into the pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
therefore, going forth to transform sentient beings is called *upāya*.
"Untainted by worldly entangments" refers to the power of *prajñā*. Furthermore, the first two phrases clarify how [the Bodhisattva] obtains his name:
because he transforms sentient beings, he is called "expedient means" (*upāya*);
the latter two phrases indicate that he transforms them without being tainted.
Furthermore, by being guided by great wisdom, compassion is rendered untainted by the defilements;
thus, one differs from ordinary worldlings.
As the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says:
Lack of wisdom combined with skillful means constitutes bondage; wisdom combined with skillful means constitutes liberation.
Because those lacking wisdom and skillful means cast themselves into the net of craving and views, they fall into the forest of signs.
Thus, "dust" refers to the sensory objects of the five desires.
"Accumulation" refers to the faults and afflictions of birth and death.
Thus, the gate of *prajñā* contemplates emptiness,
while the gate of *upāya* engages with existence.
One traverses existence without ever for a moment being deluded by emptiness;
therefore, one constantly dwells within existence yet remains unstained by it,
neither wearying of nor abandoning it, because one contemplates emptiness while within existence.
"Contemplating emptiness without realizing it" means that by relying on what preceded, one does not become stuck.
The first two phrases distinguish the provisional and the real based on the contemplation of emptiness and existence:
nirvana is emptiness, and birth-and-death is existence.
The final four lines correctly manifest non-adherence:
by means of a single mind in which the two wisdoms are mutually integrated,
one contemplates the true reality of the non-duality of emptiness and existence.
Just as one contemplates that form is "possessing form" and is therefore empty,
how could one ever momentarily be deluded regarding the emptiness of nature?
This is because one is not deluded about emptiness.
Therefore, one who constantly dwells within the realm of existence cannot be defiled by sensory objects;
the latter phrase may be understood as the opposite of this.
This is called the mutual correspondence of the two truths and the mutual support of the two practices.
Just as a chariot has two wheels and a bird has two wings,
so too must these two be present to soar through the air and travel far; if either is lacking, one is rendered incapable.
Through the gate of emptiness, one emerges from birth and death and enters nirvana;
through the gate of existence, one establishes the Buddha-dharma to transform sentient beings.
Yet, because principle and cognition are non-dual, and birth and nirvana are identical, they are as one.
It does not linger in emptiness while burdening itself with existence.
This is called the power of a single thought (ekakṣaṇabala) wherein skillful means and wisdom are fully present.
The power of a single thought is the full presence of skillful means and wisdom; "thought" here refers to the mindfulness of wisdom.
"Single" refers to the shortest possible duration.
"Skillful means" (upāya) refers to provisional wisdom, which is the aforementioned skillful means;
"wisdom" (prajñā) refers to ultimate wisdom, which is the aforementioned prajñā.
This means that in a brief moment, two types of wisdom are simultaneously present.
To speak of this again is to praise the subtlety of that wisdom.
"Excellent contemplation" (*hǎosī*) means it is clearly manifest and easily understood. "Clearly manifest" (*lìrán*) means:
The principle is extremely clear and manifest;
it can be understood with vivid clarity.
"Nirvāṇa" and "the ultimate truth" (atyanta-satya) are presented here as both the Chinese and the Indic terms.
In ancient translations, the *nirodha-satya* (truth of cessation) was rendered as the *kṣaya-satya* (truth of exhaustion).
The meaning of "exhaustion" will be explained below.
This, too, is an exegesis based on the citation of the sūtra.

This concludes the fundamental tenets of the *Anabhilāpya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Ineffable), which directly resolve [the matter] and are all-encompassing. "Resolution" (*kṣaya*) refers to all fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), as well as all karmas;
that is, the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
However, this is clarified by way of analogy.
Just as a worldly rope-knot is the most difficult to untie, so too when the principle [of this knot] is forever extinguished, birth and death are ended;
therefore, it is called "exhaustion. Birth and death constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Furthermore, these three types of defilement are also termed the "three obstructions.
These three obstructions mutually depend upon one another and are capable of obstructing nirvāṇa;
now, with reference to the path of remedy, they are collectively described as being "exhausted."
If explained individually,
such karmas as the ten non-virtuous actions can be extinguished at the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
Delusions have both a root and branches.
The "root" refers to fundamental non-enlightenment (*mūla-abodhi*), while the "branches" refer to derivative non-enlightenment.

Transcending the multitude, he ascends through the profound;
measuring the vast void, he endures forever.
Following him, one finds no trace.
When one approaches it, there is nowhere it does not look back to see its own head;
the six realms of existence cannot constrain its life,
and even the strength of the world's burden cannot transform its body.
Vast and boundless, shimmering and indistinct, it seems both present and passing away.
The five eyes cannot perceive its form;
the two ears cannot hear its sound.
Profound and obscure—who sees it, who understands it?
It encompasses all things, existing everywhere, yet it alone is drawn forth beyond the realm of existence and non-existence. (The preceding section contains nineteen sentences in total.)
The first phrase indicates the essence, while the remainder all distinguish its characteristics.
That is, the nirvana of intrinsic purity (prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa) pervades both ordinary beings and sages,
as described in the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-sūtra* under the section on the eternally true nature of the essence.
In both the first and second pairs, the preceding phrase reveals the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while the subsequent phrase reveals the detachment (*viveka*).

The "multitude of existences" refers to the twenty-five realms of existence, which are free from suffering.

The latter two phrases of the "six destinies" section concern the transcendence of arising and ceasing.
It is also free from non-self,
because the true self (ātman) of nirvāṇa possesses the sense of being a real, sovereign controller;

This is explained by way of refuting the four inversions at the final stage of the two vehicles.
"Huang" (潢) refers to a pool formed by water accumulating in a low-lying area;

Now, taking the meaning of "vast and expansive":

Thus, those who speak of it lose its truth;

Dong An Zhuanggong said: "If there is a substance, it cannot be established;

in meaning, this refers to "closing the room" (*yan-shi*).
The matters concerning the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* can be understood from that text.
As for Śakra, Brahmā, and the others,

Subhūti, relying on the analogy of magical illusions,
extensively explains the principle of the profound Prajñāpāramitā— that there is neither speaker nor listener—
up until the "Chapter on the Scattering of Flowers," where Śakra Devendra and the Four Heavenly Kings of the trichiliocosm appear.
"Transforming into celestial flowers, they scattered them over the Buddha and the great assembly," and so forth.
The meaning is that Subhūti,
through both speaking and listening, [realized] emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

"How could it be said that there is no discrimination?

"True liberation..."

Because *nirvāṇa* is not characterized by any marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

the essential meaning is that the essence of *nirvāṇa* is precisely the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of all phenomena, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

How could this text have been fabricated in vain?
For when one seeks its source by examining its objective realm,

When the five aggregates are eternally extinguished, all manifold entanglements are completely cast aside. Because all manifold entanglements are completely cast aside, one attains union with the Dao.

Because there is spiritual efficacy yet no claim of merit, the ultimate merit remains ever-present.

Because it is unimpeded yet undergoes no change, it cannot be said to possess ultimate achievement; because it exists eternally, it cannot be said to be non-existent.
The first two lines negate both existence and non-existence;

yet even this non-existence is not a realm.

It exhausts the beginning of things through the transformative mother and reaches the ultimate subtlety of the pivot of mystery. The first two phrases clarify that according to the suitability of conditions, it emerges when there is a need for birth and enters when there is a need for cessation;

Karmic retribution remains as the soul, and sacred wisdom still persists;
this is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder). There are four matters in total:

Second, the remaining traces refer to the physical body that serves as the basis.
Third, the remaining karma refers to the karma that brings about retribution, which still possesses the vital breath and spirit.

The Sūtra says:
"Smelting away dust and dross is like refining true gold;

there is nothing remaining whatsoever.

Silent and without sound;
still and without omen.

The following two phrases explain the attainment of freedom from affliction.
The six lines following "surpassing the multitude" clarify the benefits:
first, surpassing all mundane existence by being free from the marks of arising and ceasing;

Third, it is neither sound nor form;
fourth, it is ultimately non-retrogressive.
It is like a lamp whose flame has been extinguished and whose oil and light have both been exhausted.
This is *nirvāṇa* without remainder. The lamp and its flame are metaphors for the body and wisdom;

As the Sūtra says:

thus, as long as there remains something left over, there can be a designation.

they look up even more reverently to the sagely achievements.

First, because it is established by valid scriptural authority;

Thus it is said:

and where the four emptinesses are shrouded in obscurity.

the final two phrases reveal the failure to reach two types of practitioners.
It is no different from closing one's ears and eyes within the womb or eggshell, or concealing the profound man’s image beyond the clouds;
yet such people demand that the notes of *gong* and *shang* differ and insist on distinguishing between the black and the white. The profound image is like the starlight in the heavens.

These two metaphors are presented together.
